m.materie.title: Matter & the particle model
m.materie.subtitle: What is the world made of?
m.materie.goal: You understand that all substances are made up of tiny particles and can explain the three states of matter and the transitions between them.
m.materie.labTask: Examine three containers of particles: assign the correct state of matter to each particle arrangement and justify your choice in your head before you check.
m.materie.s1.title: Everything is made of particles
m.materie.s1.text:
Look around you: water, air, your pen, you yourself – everything is made up of tiny particles. They are so small that a single drop of water contains more particles than there are people on Earth – many times over!

These particles (atoms and molecules – that is, particles made of two or more atoms) are constantly in motion. How much they move and how they are arranged determines whether a substance is solid, liquid or gaseous.

Try it out: raise the temperature in the simulation container and watch what the particles do.
m.materie.s1.poe.predict: What happens to the particles when you turn the temperature up from 10° to 90° – do they get faster, bigger or more numerous? Note down your prediction before you move the slider.
m.materie.s1.poe.observe: Compare: do the particles stay the same size and the same number – and what really changes?
m.materie.s1.takeaway: All substances consist of tiny, moving particles – temperature is nothing other than particle motion.
m.materie.s2.title: The three states of matter
m.materie.s2.text:
Solid: the particles sit in fixed positions, packed tightly and in order like a honeycomb pattern. They can only jiggle (vibrate) on the spot. That is why a solid has a fixed shape.

Liquid: the particles move more freely and slide past each other – like people in a dense crowd. That is why a liquid takes on the shape of its container.

Gaseous: the particles fly fast and freely through the whole space, with lots of room between them. A gas fills any container completely.
m.materie.s2.poe.predict: Prediction: in which state are the particles furthest apart – solid, liquid or gaseous?
m.materie.s2.poe.observe: Test all three states with the slider and compare the spacing and order of the particles with your prediction.
m.materie.s2.takeaway: Solid = ordered positions · Liquid = mobile but close together · Gas = free throughout the whole space.
m.materie.s3.title: Transitions between the states
m.materie.s3.text:
When a solid is heated, its particles move more and more violently until they break free from their fixed positions: the substance melts and becomes liquid.

If the liquid is heated further, the particles become so fast that they separate from each other completely: the liquid evaporates and becomes a gas. The reverse paths are called condensing (gas → liquid) and freezing (liquid → solid).

Some substances, such as dry ice (solid CO₂), skip the liquid phase: this is called sublimation (solid → gas). The reverse path (gas → solid) is called deposition – that is how hoarfrost forms on a cold winter morning directly from water vapour.

Every pure substance has its own melting and boiling point: water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C (at normal air pressure), while iron only melts at 1538 °C. While a substance is melting or boiling, its temperature stays constant – all the added energy goes into freeing the particles from their arrangement.

Important: in all of these transitions the particles themselves never change – only their arrangement and motion!
m.materie.s3.takeaway: Melting · Evaporating · Condensing · Freezing · Subliming – in transitions only arrangement and motion change, never the particles themselves. Every pure substance has fixed melting and boiling points.
q.m1q1.question: What happens to the particles of a substance when you heat it?
q.m1q1.explanation: Heat is energy of motion: the warmer a substance, the faster its particles move. The size, mass and number of the particles stay the same.
q.m1q1.hint: Think of the particle simulation: what changed when you moved the slider – the particles themselves or their motion?
q.m1q2.question: In which state of matter are the particles most ordered?
q.m1q2.o3: The same in all of them
q.m1q2.explanation: In the solid state the particles sit in fixed positions in a regular pattern and can only vibrate.
q.m1q2.hint: In which state does a substance have a completely fixed shape that it keeps by itself?
q.m1q3.question: When water evaporates, new particles are formed.
q.m1q3.explanation: False! When water evaporates, the water particles stay exactly the same – they only separate from each other and move more freely. Physical transitions do not change the particles.
q.m1q3.hint: Separating and evaporating are physical processes – what does that mean for the particles?
q.m1q4.question: What is the transition from gas to liquid called?
q.m1q4.explanation: Condensing: the gas particles slow down and settle back together – that is how water droplets form on a cold window pane, for example.
q.m1q4.hint: Think of an example: water droplets on a cold window pane – where do they come from?
q.m1q5.question: An ice cube melts in a closed cup. What happens to the mass?
q.m1q5.explanation: When something melts, only the arrangement of the particles changes, not their number or kind. That is why the mass stays exactly the same.
q.m1q5.hint: Does the number of particles change when something melts – or only their arrangement?
m.atome.title: Atoms – the building blocks
m.atome.subtitle: Protons, neutrons, electrons
m.atome.goal: You know how an atom is built from a nucleus and an electron cloud, and you can build an atom yourself from its data.
m.atome.labTask: Build three atoms to specification: set the right numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons. Tip: atomic number = protons, mass number = protons + neutrons.
m.atome.s1.title: The structure of the atom
m.atome.s1.text:
Every atom consists of two regions: the tiny, heavy atomic nucleus in the middle and the huge, almost empty electron cloud around it.

The nucleus holds the protons (positively charged) and the neutrons (neutral). In the cloud, the electrons (negatively charged) whizz around the nucleus on fixed paths called shells – more on that in a moment.

For a sense of scale: if the nucleus were the size of a cherry in the middle of a football stadium, the electrons would be tiny specks of dust up in the stands. In between: nothing!
m.atome.s1.poe.predict: Prediction: where is most of an atom's mass – in the nucleus or in the electron cloud?
m.atome.s1.poe.observe: Select different elements in the explorer: which changes more – the numbers in the nucleus (p⁺, n) or the number of electrons?
m.atome.s1.takeaway: Atom = tiny, heavy nucleus (p⁺, n) + huge, almost empty cloud with electrons.
m.atome.s2.title: Charge and atomic number
m.atome.s2.text:
The number of protons determines which element an atom is. It is called the atomic number: 1 proton = hydrogen, 6 protons = carbon, 8 protons = oxygen. Every element has an element symbol of one or two letters that is the same all over the world: H, C, O. Some symbols come from Latin – for example Fe for iron (ferrum) or Au for gold (aurum).

A neutral atom always has as many electrons as protons – the charges cancel out. If there are more or fewer electrons, the atom is charged and is called an ion (more on that in Module 4).

The neutrons keep the nucleus stable. Protons + neutrons together give the mass number, because almost all of the mass sits in the nucleus.

Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons – such variants are called isotopes. Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons, carbon-14 has 8; both are carbon because both have 6 protons. That is why the periodic table often shows an “odd” atomic mass (chlorine: 35.5): it is the average of all naturally occurring isotopes.
m.atome.s2.takeaway: Atomic number = number of protons = element. Neutral atoms: electrons = protons. Mass number = p + n. Isotopes: same element, different number of neutrons.
m.atome.s3.title: Electrons on shells
m.atome.s3.text:
Electrons do not move around at random but on fixed shells around the nucleus – like the floors of a building. (This shell model is a simplification: in reality you can only say where an electron is likely to be. For school chemistry, however, the model is perfectly sufficient.)

The first shell holds at most 2 electrons, the second 8, the third also 8 (for the first 20 elements). Only when a shell is full is the next one filled.

The electrons on the outermost shell are called valence electrons (valence = ability to bond). They alone decide how an element reacts and bonds – that is what Module 4 is about!
m.atome.s3.poe.predict: Prediction: how many electrons fit on the second shell at most?
m.atome.s3.poe.observe: In the explorer, select elements 3–10 in order and watch which element the third shell starts with.
m.atome.s3.takeaway: Shells fill from the inside out: 2 – 8 – 8. The outermost electrons (valence electrons) determine chemical behaviour.
q.m2q1.question: Where is almost the entire mass of an atom?
q.m2q1.explanation: Protons and neutrons are around 2000 times heavier than electrons – and both sit in the nucleus. The electron cloud is almost massless empty space.
q.m2q1.hint: Compare the masses: protons and neutrons are around 2000 times heavier than electrons. Where do p and n sit?
q.m2q2.question: An atom has 6 protons. Which element is it?
q.m2q2.explanation: The number of protons (atomic number) determines the element: 6 protons = carbon (C).
q.m2q2.hint: The number of protons is the atomic number – which element has atomic number 6?
q.m2q3.question: A neutral atom always has the same number of electrons as protons.
q.m2q3.explanation: True! Positive protons and negative electrons cancel each other out – otherwise the atom would be charged (an ion).
q.m2q3.hint: What happens to the total charge when positive and negative charges occur equally often?
q.m2q4.question: An oxygen atom has 8 protons and the mass number 16. How many neutrons does it have?
q.m2q4.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons. So: 16 − 8 = 8 neutrons.
q.m2q4.hint: Mass number = protons + neutrons. Rearrange the equation to get the neutrons.
q.m2q5.question: Why is the outermost electron shell so important?
q.m2q5.o2: It protects the nucleus from water
q.m2q5.o3: It gives the atom its colour
q.m2q5.explanation: The valence electrons on the outermost shell decide whether and how an atom forms bonds and reacts.
q.m2q5.hint: On which shell do bonds happen – the innermost or the outermost?
m.periodensystem.title: The periodic table
m.periodensystem.subtitle: The map of the elements
m.periodensystem.goal: You can find elements in the periodic table and read off their properties from their position.
m.periodensystem.labTask: Find three elements in the periodic table using the clues. Use what you know about groups and periods – then click the right box.
m.periodensystem.s1.title: One system for all the elements
m.periodensystem.s1.text:
There are 118 known elements – around 90 of them occur in nature, the rest were made artificially. The periodic table (PT) arranges them all: not at random, but by atomic number and properties.

It is like a map of chemistry: if you can read where an element sits, you already know a lot about it without ever having seen it.

Click on different elements in the periodic table and look at their profiles. The lab shows the first 20 elements – the most important ones to start with.
m.periodensystem.s1.poe.predict: Prediction: what does an element's reactivity depend on more – its mass or its position in the periodic table?
m.periodensystem.s1.poe.observe: Click on elements of the same group (e.g. Li, Na, K) and compare their valence electrons. What do they have in common?
m.periodensystem.s1.takeaway: The periodic table is ordered by atomic number – if you can read the position, you know the properties.
m.periodensystem.s2.title: Groups and periods
m.periodensystem.s2.text:
The vertical columns are called groups. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons – and therefore resemble each other strongly: the alkali metals in group 1 react violently with water, the noble gases in group 18 hardly react at all. (Hydrogen sits at the very top of group 1, but it is a non-metal and not an alkali metal – a special case.)

The horizontal rows are called periods. From left to right the number of protons increases by 1 per box, and all elements of a period have the same number of electron shells.

Example: sodium (Na) is in group 1, period 3 – so it has 1 valence electron on the third shell.

By the way: groups 3 to 12 (the transition metals such as iron, copper or gold) only begin in period 4. That is why the periodic table has a big gap in the middle of the first three periods. As a rough rule: metals are on the left and at the bottom, non-metals at the top right – with the semimetals in between.
m.periodensystem.s2.takeaway: Group (vertical) = same valence electrons = similar properties · Period (horizontal) = same number of shells.
m.periodensystem.s3.title: Important element families
m.periodensystem.s3.text:
Alkali metals (group 1): soft, light metals, extremely reactive. Sodium in water = spectacular reaction!

Alkaline earth metals (group 2): magnesium and calcium – also reactive metals, but tamer than group 1. Calcium is found in bones and limestone, magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame.

Halogens (group 17): aggressive non-metals such as chlorine and fluorine, which are exactly 1 electron short of a full shell.

Noble gases (group 18): full outer shell, therefore completely content and unreactive – perfect for balloons and neon tubes.

The elements in between – metals, semimetals, non-metals – are best explored yourself in the periodic table.
m.periodensystem.s3.takeaway: Group 1 reacts violently, group 17 is looking for 1 electron, group 18 wants nothing at all – a full shell makes an atom content.
q.m3q1.question: What is the periodic table essentially arranged by?
q.m3q1.explanation: The elements are arranged by increasing atomic number (number of protons) – from H (1) up to the heaviest elements.
q.m3q1.hint: The boxes are numbered in order – what does this number count in an atom?
q.m3q2.question: What do elements in the same group have in common?
q.m3q2.o1: The same number of valence electrons and similar properties
q.m3q2.explanation: Members of a group have the same number of electrons on the outermost shell – that is why their chemical properties are so similar.
q.m3q2.hint: Compare Li, Na and K in the periodic table: what do all three in group 1 have the same?
q.m3q3.question: Noble gases are especially keen to react with other substances.
q.m3q3.explanation: False! Noble gases have a full outer shell and are therefore chemically content – they hardly form any bonds.
q.m3q3.hint: Remember the octet rule: what does the outer shell of the noble gases look like?
q.m3q4.question: Chlorine is in group 17. How many valence electrons does it have?
q.m3q4.explanation: For groups 13–18, the last digit of the group number gives the number of valence electrons: group 17 → 7 valence electrons.
q.m3q4.hint: For groups 13–18, the last digit of the group number is what counts. Group 17 → ?
q.m3q5.question: Which element is an alkali metal?
q.m3q5.explanation: Like lithium and sodium, potassium is in group 1 – the alkali metals. Magnesium belongs to the alkaline earth metals (group 2).
q.m3q5.hint: The alkali metals are all in the same group – which one?
m.bindungen.title: Chemical bonds
m.bindungen.subtitle: Why atoms stick together
m.bindungen.goal: You understand the octet rule and can tell ionic bonds and covalent bonds apart and explain them.
m.bindungen.labTask: Decide for four pairs of substances which type of bond forms. Ask yourself first: are they metals or non-metals? Which one wants to give electrons away, which one wants to take them up, which ones want to share?
m.bindungen.s1.title: The octet rule: striving for a full shell
m.bindungen.s1.text:
A bond is a firm connection between atoms. Why do atoms form bonds at all? The answer lies in their valence electrons: atoms strive to have a full outer shell – usually 8 electrons (the octet rule), just like the content noble gases.

To reach this goal, atoms have two strategies: give electrons away or take them up completely (→ ionic bond), or share electrons (→ covalent bond).

In the lab, watch how sodium and chlorine become partners.
m.bindungen.s1.poe.predict: Prediction: why does sodium prefer to give its electron away rather than take up 7?
m.bindungen.s1.poe.observe: Follow the NaCl simulation step by step: count the electrons on the outer shells of both atoms before and after the transfer.
m.bindungen.s1.takeaway: Atoms strive for a full outer shell (octet rule) – to get there, they give, take or share electrons.
m.bindungen.s2.title: Ionic bond: giving and taking
m.bindungen.s2.text:
Sodium has 1 valence electron too many, chlorine is exactly 1 short. The way out: sodium hands its electron over to chlorine.

This creates ions: sodium becomes the positively charged Na⁺ (one electron lost), chlorine the negative Cl⁻ (one electron gained). Positive ions are called cations, negative ones anions.

Because opposite charges attract, the ions cling firmly to each other – that is the ionic bond. They do not form single pairs but a huge, regular ionic lattice of countless ions: a salt crystal. That is how table salt, NaCl, is formed.

Typical: ionic bonds form between metals (which give electrons away) and non-metals (which take them up). That is why salts are hard, brittle and have high melting points – table salt only melts at 801 °C. Dissolved in water or molten, they conduct electricity because the ions can then move freely.
m.bindungen.s2.takeaway: Metal gives electrons away (+), non-metal takes them up (−) – the attraction between the charges holds the ions together.
m.bindungen.s3.title: Covalent bond: sharing instead of swapping
m.bindungen.s3.text:
Two hydrogen atoms both have 1 electron – neither wants to give it away. So they share: each contributes 1 electron to a shared electron pair. That way each atom has 2 electrons around it – the first shell is full.

These shared electron pairs are the covalent bond (also called atomic bond). This is how molecules such as H₂, O₂ or H₂O are formed.

Typical: covalent bonds form between non-metals. Oxygen, for example, needs 2 electron pairs → O₂ has a double bond, H₂O has two single bonds.

And metal + metal? That is the third type of bond, the metallic bond: all metal atoms release their valence electrons into a shared “electron gas” that holds the positive atomic cores together. These freely moving electrons are the reason why metals conduct electricity and heat so well and can be bent without breaking.
m.bindungen.s3.takeaway: Non-metal + non-metal = covalent bond (sharing electron pairs) · Metal + non-metal = ionic bond · Metal + metal = metallic bond (electron gas).
q.m4q1.question: What is the goal of the octet rule?
q.m4q1.o0: To have 8 protons in the nucleus
q.m4q1.o1: To reach a full outer electron shell
q.m4q1.explanation: Atoms strive for 8 valence electrons (2 for the first shell) – the stable noble gas configuration.
q.m4q1.hint: What do all noble gases have in common that makes them so unreactive?
q.m4q2.question: Sodium gives away an electron. What charge does the resulting ion have?
q.m4q2.explanation: If a neutral atom loses a negative electron, a surplus of positive protons is left over: Na⁺.
q.m4q2.hint: An electron is negatively charged. What is left when a neutral atom loses one?
q.m4q3.question: In a covalent bond, electrons are transferred completely from one atom to the other.
q.m4q3.explanation: False – that is the ionic bond! In a covalent bond, the atoms share electron pairs.
q.m4q3.hint: Tell the two strategies apart: transferring completely vs. sharing – which one was the covalent bond?
q.m4q4.question: Which bond typically forms between magnesium (metal) and oxygen (non-metal)?
q.m4q4.explanation: Metal + non-metal → the classic case for an ionic bond. Magnesium hands 2 electrons over to oxygen: MgO.
q.m4q4.hint: Rule to remember: metal + non-metal → one of the two types of bond. Which one?
q.m4q5.question: Two hydrogen atoms form H₂. What holds them together?
q.m4q5.explanation: Both atoms share an electron pair (covalent bond), so that each one has a full first shell with 2 electrons.
q.m4q5.hint: Both hydrogen atoms want 1 more electron each – how do they manage that without giving one away?
m.formeln.title: Molecules & formulas
m.formeln.subtitle: Reading the language of chemistry
m.formeln.goal: You can read chemical formulas, count atoms and know what distinguishes molecules from compounds.
m.formeln.labTask: Count the atoms in three formulas of real chemicals. Write down the correct number for each element – and watch out for the brackets!
m.formeln.s1.title: Molecules and compounds
m.formeln.s1.text:
When atoms join through covalent bonds, molecules are formed: the smallest particles made of at least two atoms.

A molecule can consist of identical atoms (O₂ – oxygen molecule) or of different ones (H₂O – water molecule). Substances made of at least two different elements are called compounds.

Remember: not every molecule is a compound. O₂ is a molecule, but not a compound – it consists of only one element.

And salts such as NaCl? They do not form molecules but an ionic lattice (Module 4). Their formula is a ratio formula: NaCl means “Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a 1 : 1 ratio”, not “one particle made of two atoms”.
m.formeln.s1.takeaway: Molecule = at least 2 atoms · Compound = at least 2 different elements. O₂ is a molecule but not a compound; NaCl is a compound but not a molecule.
m.formeln.s2.title: Reading chemical formulas
m.formeln.s2.text:
Chemists write molecules as formulas – an international shorthand. H₂O means: 2 hydrogen atoms (H) + 1 oxygen atom (O).

The small lowered number (the subscript) always applies to the element directly before it. No number = 1 atom.

Examples: CO₂ = 1 carbon + 2 oxygen. NH₃ (ammonia) = 1 nitrogen + 3 hydrogen. C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) = 6 C + 12 H + 6 O.

Watch out for brackets: Ca(OH)₂ means the bracket occurs 2 times → 1 Ca, 2 O, 2 H!
m.formeln.s2.poe.predict: Prediction: how many atoms are in Ca(OH)₂ – does the 2 count only the H or the whole bracket?
m.formeln.s2.poe.observe: Open the formula reader for calcium hydroxide and compare with your count: 1 Ca, 2 O, 2 H.
m.formeln.s2.takeaway: The subscript applies to the element directly before it; a subscript after a bracket multiplies everything inside it.
m.formeln.s3.title: Why formulas are so useful
m.formeln.s3.text:
Formulas are more than abbreviations – they reveal the exact composition of a substance. From that you can tell what can happen in reactions.

Example: methane CH₄ burns with oxygen O₂ to form CO₂ and H₂O. The formulas show you straight away which atoms have to end up where.

What is more, chemists all over the world understand the same formulas – whether in Zurich, Tokyo or Nairobi. H₂O needs no translation!
m.formeln.s3.takeaway: Formulas reveal the exact composition – they are the international language of chemistry.
q.m5q1.question: How many atoms are there in total in one H₂SO₄ molecule (sulfuric acid)?
q.m5q1.hint: Count element by element: H₂ = 2, then S, then O₄ – and add it all up.
q.m5q2.question: What does the subscript number in CO₂ mean?
q.m5q2.o1: There are 2 oxygen atoms per molecule
q.m5q2.o2: The molecule is twice as heavy
q.m5q2.explanation: The subscript applies to the element directly before it: CO₂ has 1 C atom and 2 O atoms.
q.m5q2.hint: The subscript comes directly AFTER an element – which one does it apply to here?
q.m5q3.question: O₂ is a compound.
q.m5q3.explanation: False! O₂ is a molecule, but it consists of only one element. Compounds contain at least two different elements.
q.m5q3.hint: What is O₂ made of – one element or several different elements?
q.m5q4.question: How many hydrogen atoms does Ca(OH)₂ contain?
q.m5q4.explanation: The bracket (OH) occurs 2 times: 2 × 1 H = 2 hydrogen atoms (and likewise 2 O atoms).
q.m5q4.hint: The 2 after the bracket applies to EVERYTHING inside the bracket – so to the H as well.
q.m5q5.question: Which formula describes a molecule with 2 nitrogen and 5 oxygen atoms?
q.m5q5.explanation: The subscript comes directly after the element: N₂O₅ = 2 N + 5 O. (A number IN FRONT of the formula would count whole molecules – more on that in Module 6!)
q.m5q5.hint: The subscript belongs to the element directly before it: 2 N and 5 O – how do you write that?
m.reaktionen.title: Chemical reactions
m.reaktionen.subtitle: When substances transform
m.reaktionen.goal: You understand what happens in a chemical reaction and can balance reaction equations.
m.reaktionen.labTask: Balance three reaction equations – from easy to tricky. Count the atoms on both sides and work out which coefficient fixes the balance.
m.reaktionen.s1.title: What is a chemical reaction?
m.reaktionen.s1.text:
In physical processes (melting, evaporating, dissolving) the particles stay the same. In chemical reactions, on the other hand, bonds are broken and formed anew – new substances with new properties are created.

Signs of this: colour change, gas formation, temperature change, precipitate or smell. Iron rusting, wood burning, fruit rotting – chemical reactions are happening everywhere. Another difference: physical processes are easy to reverse (melted ice freezes again), chemical reactions usually are not – ash does not turn back into wood.

The starting substances are called reactants (or educts), the newly formed substances products (from Latin producere = to bring forth).
m.reaktionen.s1.takeaway: Chemical = new substances are formed (bonds are made anew) · Physical = same particles, new form.
m.reaktionen.s2.title: Reaction equations: the balance must be right
m.reaktionen.s2.text:
Chemists write reactions as an equation: reactants → products. Example, the formation of water:

hydrogen + oxygen → water, as a formula: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O

But wait – that is not right yet! There are 2 O atoms on the left, only 1 on the right. Atoms, however, can neither vanish nor appear out of nothing. This is the law of conservation of mass, which Antoine Lavoisier discovered at the end of the 18th century by careful weighing: the mass of the products always equals the mass of the reactants.

The trick: coefficients are placed in front of the formulas: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. A coefficient applies to the whole formula after it – 2 H₂O means 2 water molecules with a total of 4 H and 2 O atoms. Now both sides count 4 H and 2 O. This is called balancing. Important: only change the coefficients – never the subscripts! And in the end you choose the smallest possible whole numbers: 4 H₂ + 2 O₂ → 4 H₂O would also be balanced, but is reduced by dividing by 2.
m.reaktionen.s2.poe.predict: Prediction: are you allowed to change the small subscripts in the formulas when balancing – yes or no?
m.reaktionen.s2.poe.observe: In the workshop, deliberately set some wrong coefficients and watch the atom counters: what always has to match on the left and right?
m.reaktionen.s2.takeaway: Balancing means: only adjust the coefficients, never the subscripts – each element must appear the same number of times on the left and on the right.
m.reaktionen.s3.title: A strategy for balancing
m.reaktionen.s3.text:
Balancing is like a puzzle – with a system it becomes easy:

1. Count the atoms of each element on both sides.
2. Start with an element that appears in only one substance on each side.
3. Adjust the coefficients and count again – one change often affects several elements.
4. Hydrogen and oxygen usually come last.

Example: CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Carbon is already right (1 : 1). Hydrogen: 4 on the left, 2 on the right → 2 H₂O. Now oxygen: 2 + 2 = 4 on the right → 2 O₂. Done: CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O!

Try it yourself right away in the equation workshop.
m.reaktionen.s3.takeaway: Count first, then balance element by element – hydrogen and oxygen last.
q.m6q1.question: What is a sure sign of a chemical reaction?
q.m6q1.explanation: The heart of every chemical reaction: new substances with new properties are formed. Changes of shape or state alone are physical.
q.m6q1.hint: What sets a chemical change apart from a physical one? Does the substance stay the same?
q.m6q2.question: Why do reaction equations have to be balanced?
q.m6q2.o1: Because atoms can neither appear nor disappear
q.m6q2.o2: So that the reaction runs faster
q.m6q2.o3: Because the law of gravity demands it
q.m6q2.explanation: Conservation of mass: before and after the reaction, the number of each kind of atom must be the same – atoms only swap partners.
q.m6q2.hint: Atoms can neither disappear nor be created in a reaction – what does that mean for the equation?
q.m6q3.question: When balancing, you are allowed to change the subscripts in the formulas.
q.m6q3.explanation: Never! The subscript defines the substance: H₂O would suddenly become H₂O₂, hydrogen peroxide. Only the coefficients in front are changed.
q.m6q3.hint: What would become of H₂O if you changed the 2 on the O? Still water?
q.m6q4.question: Balance: __ Fe + __ O₂ → __ Fe₂O₃
q.m6q4.explanation: Oxygen: the lowest common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6 → 3 O₂ and 2 Fe₂O₃. Then iron: 2 × 2 = 4 Fe. Balanced!
q.m6q4.hint: Count oxygen: O₂ on the left, O₃ on the right. Find the lowest common multiple of 2 and 3.
q.m6q5.question: In the equation 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, the reactants are …
q.m6q5.explanation: Reactants are on the left of the arrow (the starting substances), products on the right. Here: hydrogen and oxygen are the reactants.
q.m6q5.hint: Reactants = starting substances. Are they before or after the arrow?
m.ph.title: Acids, bases & pH
m.ph.subtitle: From lemons to soap
m.ph.goal: You know what acids and bases are, can place a pH value on the scale and work with indicators.
m.ph.labTask: Sort five everyday substances by their pH value into acidic, neutral or basic. Use the virtual lab to test each substance before you decide!
m.ph.s1.title: Acids and bases in everyday life
m.ph.s1.text:
You meet acids and bases all the time: lemon juice, vinegar, cola and descaler are acidic; soap, baking soda and drain cleaner are basic (also called alkaline).

Acids taste sour (never taste anything in the lab!) and can attack materials – strong acids even skin and metal. That is exactly why acidic descaler dissolves the limescale in a coffee machine. A base is the chemical opponent of an acid; its solution in water is called a lye or alkaline solution. Bases often feel soapy-slippery and can be corrosive too.

What is behind it chemically? In water, acids release hydrogen ions (H⁺) – the more H⁺ ions, the more acidic. Alkaline solutions contain hydroxide ions (OH⁻). When the two meet, they combine to form water: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. This is neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution, for example, give a solution of table salt – and that is why slightly basic toothpaste helps against the acid that bacteria produce on your teeth.
m.ph.s1.poe.predict: Prediction: is soap below or above pH 7 – and why does it feel slippery?
m.ph.s1.poe.observe: In the pH lab, test lemon juice, water and soap solution: what colour does the indicator show for each?
m.ph.s1.takeaway: pH < 7 acidic (H⁺ ions) · pH = 7 neutral · pH > 7 basic (OH⁻ ions) – acid + base neutralise each other to salt and water.
m.ph.s2.title: The pH scale
m.ph.s2.text:
How acidic or basic a solution is, is measured by the pH value – a scale from 0 to 14. Behind it is the concentration of H⁺ ions: the more there are, the lower the pH.

pH below 7 = acidic (the lower, the more acidic)
pH exactly 7 = neutral (pure water)
pH above 7 = basic (the higher, the more basic)

The scale is logarithmic: pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4 and a hundred times more acidic than pH 5! Stomach acid (pH ~1.5) is therefore really fierce – luckily a layer of mucus protects our stomach.

Slide through various everyday substances in the lab and look at their pH.
m.ph.s2.takeaway: The scale is logarithmic: each pH unit means a factor of 10.
m.ph.s3.title: Indicators: chemistry you can see
m.ph.s3.text:
How do you recognise the pH value? With indicators – substances that change colour depending on the pH. The best known: universal indicator, a colour gradient from red (acidic) through green (neutral) to violet (strongly basic).

Nature helps too: red cabbage juice turns red in acid and blue-green in base. And hydrangeas bloom blue on acidic soil and pink on basic soil – a living pH meter in the garden!

Indicators only give an approximate pH – pH paper is nothing more than indicator on a paper strip. To measure it precisely you use an electronic pH meter.
m.ph.s3.takeaway: Indicators change colour depending on the pH – universal indicator: red = acidic, green = neutral, violet = basic.
q.m7q1.question: A solution has pH 3. It is …
q.m7q1.explanation: Everything below pH 7 is acidic – and pH 3 is well below that, so clearly acidic (like vinegar or cola).
q.m7q1.hint: The middle of the scale is 7 = neutral. Which side of 7 is 3 on?
q.m7q2.question: What happens when you mix an acid with exactly the right amount of base?
q.m7q2.o1: They neutralise each other to salt and water
q.m7q2.explanation: Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. The pH value moves towards the middle at 7.
q.m7q2.hint: Acid and base are opponents – what does combining them give in a neutralisation?
q.m7q3.question: A solution with pH 2 is ten times more acidic than one with pH 3.
q.m7q3.explanation: True! The pH scale is logarithmic: each unit means a factor of 10.
q.m7q3.hint: The scale is logarithmic: what does a difference of 1 pH unit mean?
q.m7q4.question: Which everyday substance is basic?
q.m7q4.explanation: Soap is basic (pH ~10) – that is why it feels slippery. Lemon, vinegar and cola are acids.
q.m7q4.hint: Three of the four substances taste sour – which one feels slippery and soapy instead?
q.m7q5.question: Universal indicator turns a solution green. What does that mean?
q.m7q5.explanation: Green is in the middle of the indicator scale: pH 7, neutral – like pure water.
q.m7q5.hint: Think of the colour gradient: red = acidic, violet = basic – what is in the middle?
m.trennung.title: Mixtures & separation methods
m.trennung.subtitle: Salt, sand and clever tricks
m.trennung.goal: You can tell pure substances from mixtures and choose the right separation method for a mixture.
m.trennung.labTask: Four mixtures are waiting in the lab. Choose the right separation method for each – think first about which property of the substances you can make use of!
m.trennung.s1.title: Pure substance or mixture?
m.trennung.s1.text:
A pure substance consists of only one kind of particle – for example pure water (only H₂O molecules) or pure gold. A mixture contains several substances that are physically mixed but not chemically bonded to each other.

In heterogeneous mixtures you can see the components: sand in water, oil droplets in vinegar. Homogeneous mixtures look uniform even though they are mixed: salt water, air or brass.

The crucial point: because the particles in a mixture are not bonded, you can separate them from each other again with physical tricks.
m.trennung.s1.poe.predict: Prediction: is salt water a pure substance? It does look completely uniform …
m.trennung.s1.poe.observe: Look at the salt water example in the separation explorer: why can it be separated by evaporation if it were just one substance?
m.trennung.s1.takeaway: Pure substance = one kind of particle · Mixture = several substances, physically mixed and therefore separable.
m.trennung.s2.title: Separating using the properties of substances
m.trennung.s2.text:
Every separation method makes use of a different property of the substances:

Filtering uses particle size: grains of sand get stuck in the filter paper, water runs through. This is how insoluble solids are separated from liquids.

Evaporating uses the boiling point: if you heat salt water, the water evaporates – the salt remains as crystals. This is how you recover the dissolved solid.

The magnet uses magnetism: iron filings can simply be pulled out of sand, without any water at all.

Other classics: sedimentation and decanting use density – sand sinks to the bottom in water, then you carefully pour off the clear water. Extraction uses solubility: hot water dissolves the flavour compounds out of tea leaves or ground coffee.
m.trennung.s2.takeaway: Every separation method uses one property: filter = particle size · evaporating = boiling point · magnet = magnetism · sedimentation = density · extraction = solubility.
m.trennung.s3.title: Distillation and chromatography
m.trennung.s3.text:
What if you want to keep both substances? In distillation, the liquid is evaporated and the vapour is collected again in a second, cooled vessel. This is how you separate liquids with different boiling points – for example alcohol (boils at 78 °C) from water (100 °C).

Chromatography separates substances by how fast they "travel" on paper: it splits black ink into blue, red and yellow. Forensic scientists use the same technique to compare inks!

Just as important as in Module 1: all separation methods are physical processes. The particles themselves never change – you only sort them.
m.trennung.s3.takeaway: Distillation separates by boiling point and collects the vapour again – chromatography by how fast the dyes travel.
q.m8q1.question: Salt water is …
q.m8q1.explanation: Salt water looks uniform but contains two substances (water + salt) that are not chemically bonded: a homogeneous mixture.
q.m8q1.hint: It looks uniform but contains two substances – what is such a mixture called?
q.m8q2.question: What is the best way to separate sand from water?
q.m8q2.explanation: Sand is insoluble: the grains get stuck in the filter paper, the water runs through. Filtering uses particle size.
q.m8q2.hint: Sand does not dissolve in water – which method uses particle size?
q.m8q3.question: When a mixture is separated, the particles are changed chemically.
q.m8q3.explanation: False! Separation methods are physical processes: the particles stay exactly the same – they are only sorted.
q.m8q3.hint: Remember Module 1: do physical processes change the particles – or not?
q.m8q4.question: You want to get the salt out of salt water (you do not care about the water). Which method?
q.m8q4.explanation: When evaporating, the water disappears as vapour and the dissolved salt is left behind as crystals – that is how sea salt is produced.
q.m8q4.hint: The salt is dissolved, not in pieces – so filtering will not work. What happens when you heat it?
q.m8q5.question: Distillation separates two liquids because they …
q.m8q5.explanation: The liquid with the lower boiling point evaporates first and is collected again as a liquid in the cooled part of the apparatus.
q.m8q5.hint: In distillation, the liquid that evaporates first is the one with the lower …?
m.energie.title: Energy & speed
m.energie.subtitle: Why reactions are hot, cold, fast or sluggish
m.energie.goal: You can tell exothermic and endothermic reactions apart and use the particle model to explain how reactions can be sped up.
m.energie.labTask: Magnesium reacts with acid – how fast is up to you. Set the temperature, concentration and degree of division so that the reaction is finished in 1 second!
m.energie.s1.title: Exothermic and endothermic
m.energie.s1.text:
Every chemical reaction exchanges energy. Exothermic reactions release energy as heat: fireworks, burning wood, hand-warmer pads. It gets warm.

Endothermic reactions draw energy from their surroundings: a cold pack from the pharmacy becomes ice-cold because the reaction inside “eats” heat. Photosynthesis is endothermic too – plants put light energy into building glucose.

In the lab you see this as an energy diagram: if the products lie lower than the reactants, energy was released (exothermic). The “hill” in between is the activation energy: even an exothermic reaction usually needs a push to get started – wood does not burn by itself until the match supplies the first bit of energy. After that, the reaction supplies the energy for the rest itself.

Energy is never lost in the process: it is either stored in the bonds of the substances (chemical energy) or released as heat, light or motion.
m.energie.s1.poe.predict: Prediction: if the products lie lower in energy than the reactants – does it get warm or cold?
m.energie.s1.poe.observe: Switch the energy diagram between exothermic and endothermic and compare: where does the energy level of the products lie in each case?
m.energie.s1.takeaway: Exothermic gives off heat (products lower) · Endothermic takes in heat (products higher).
m.energie.s2.title: Reaction rate in the particle model
m.energie.s2.text:
For particles to react, they have to collide with enough energy – like billiard balls that must hit each other hard enough. From this follow three levers for the speed (a fourth one, the catalyst, you will meet in the next step):

Temperature: hotter particles are faster → more collisions, and more collisions with enough energy. Rule of thumb: 10 °C warmer doubles to quadruples the speed of many reactions.

Concentration (how many particles per volume): more particles in the same space → more frequent collisions.

Surface area (degree of division): powder has far more surface to attack than a lump → flour dust can even explode, while a cereal bar just lies there quietly.
m.energie.s2.poe.predict: Prediction: which has the bigger effect – doubling the temperature or doubling the concentration?
m.energie.s2.poe.observe: In the speed lab, turn up the factors one at a time and watch the bubbles: how much does each slider change the relative speed?
m.energie.s2.takeaway: Reacting needs collisions with enough energy – temperature, concentration and surface area increase the collision rate.
m.energie.s3.title: The catalyst: turbo without being used up
m.energie.s3.text:
A catalyst makes reactions faster without being used up itself. It lowers the energy hurdle that particles have to overcome when they collide – the activation energy – like a tunnel through a mountain instead of the path over it.

Catalysts are everywhere in everyday life: the catalytic converter in a car cleans the exhaust gases, enzymes in your saliva break down starch while you are still eating, and enzymes in washing powder dissolve stains at just 30 °C.

You know the opposite from the kitchen: the fridge slows down rotting, because cold slows down all reactions.
m.energie.s3.takeaway: The catalyst lowers the activation energy and comes out of the reaction unchanged.
q.m9q1.question: An exothermic reaction …
q.m9q1.o0: gives off heat to its surroundings
q.m9q1.explanation: Exo = out: the products lie lower in energy than the reactants, and the difference is released as heat – as in burning, for example.
q.m9q1.hint: Exo = out, endo = in – which way does the heat flow in “exothermic”?
q.m9q2.question: A catalyst is used up in the reaction.
q.m9q2.explanation: False! The catalyst speeds up the reaction but comes out of it unchanged – that is why a small amount is enough.
q.m9q2.hint: The catalyst is like a tunnel through the mountain – does the tunnel get used up when you drive through it?
q.m9q3.question: Why does a powder react faster than a lump of the same substance?
q.m9q3.o1: Powder has a much larger surface area
q.m9q3.o2: Powder particles are smaller than atoms
q.m9q3.explanation: Reactions take place at the surface. Powder offers the colliding particles an enormous amount of surface to attack – so more collisions per unit of time.
q.m9q3.hint: Reactions take place at the surface – which has more surface: a lump or a powder?
q.m9q4.question: You raise the temperature. What happens in the particle model?
q.m9q4.o1: The particles collide more often and with more energy
q.m9q4.explanation: Higher temperature = faster particles = more collisions, and more of them with enough energy to react.
q.m9q4.hint: Temperature is particle motion – what do faster particles mean for the collisions?
q.m9q5.question: A cold pack gets ice-cold when activated. The reaction inside it is …
q.m9q5.explanation: Endothermic: the reaction draws heat from its surroundings (and from your sprained ankle) – that is why it gets cold.
q.m9q5.hint: The pack gets cold because the reaction draws heat from its surroundings – what is that called?
m.mol.title: The mole
m.mol.subtitle: Weighing instead of counting
m.mol.goal: You know what a mole is, can calculate with molar mass and read balanced equations as "recipes".
m.mol.labTask: Four calculations from the lab ticket: convert between grams and moles and read an equation as a recipe. Keep the formula in mind: m = n · M!
m.mol.s1.title: Weighing instead of counting
m.mol.s1.text:
A drop of water contains more particles than a person could count – even in a thousand lifetimes. That is why chemists do not count particles one by one but weigh them: they pack huge, fixed quantities into bundles.

Such a bundle is the mole: 1 mole = 6.022 · 10²³ particles. That is the Avogadro constant – roughly a 6 followed by 23 zeros. For comparison: 1 mole of peas would cover the entire surface of the Earth, oceans included, several hundred metres deep.

The amount of substance n therefore tells you how many such bundles you have – like “dozen”, only for particles: 2 mol of water = 2 × 6.022 · 10²³ water molecules.
m.mol.s1.takeaway: 1 mole = 6.022 · 10²³ particles – the amount of substance n counts huge bundles of particles instead of individual particles.
m.mol.s2.title: Molar mass
m.mol.s2.text:
How heavy is such a mole? Conveniently, that is written in the periodic table: the atomic mass of an element (in the unit u) is numerically equal to the mass of 1 mole in grams. 1 mole of carbon (atomic mass 12 u) weighs 12 g, 1 mole of oxygen (16 u) weighs 16 g – and 1 mole of chlorine (35.5 u) weighs 35.5 g.

For molecules you simply add up: water H₂O = 2 × 1 + 16 = 18 g/mol. CO₂ = 12 + 2 × 16 = 44 g/mol. This number is called the molar mass M.

With it you convert: mass = amount of substance × molar mass, in short m = n · M. Example: 0.5 mol of water weighs 0.5 × 18 = 9 g. The other way round: n = m / M – 36 g of water is 36 / 18 = 2 mol.
m.mol.s2.poe.predict: Prediction: which weighs more – 1 mol of H₂O or 1 mol of CO₂?
m.mol.s2.poe.observe: Set the mole scale to 1 mol of each and compare the masses: explain the difference using the atomic masses.
m.mol.s2.takeaway: M = sum of the atomic masses (g/mol) · m = n · M or n = m / M – the atomic mass in the periodic table tells you the molar mass.
m.mol.s3.title: Reading equations as recipes
m.mol.s3.text:
This brings us full circle back to Module 6: a balanced equation is a recipe in moles. 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O means: 2 mol of hydrogen + 1 mol of oxygen give 2 mol of water.

This is how chemists work out how much they need to weigh out: if you want to make 2 mol of water (36 g), you need 2 mol of H₂ (4 g) and 1 mol of O₂ (32 g). Not a gram too much, not a gram too little – conservation of mass in action.

By the way: 4 g + 32 g = 36 g. The balance always adds up!
m.mol.s3.takeaway: Coefficients = mole ratios: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O means 2 mol + 1 mol give 2 mol.
q.m10q1.question: How many particles are there in 1 mole?
q.m10q1.explanation: The Avogadro constant applies to every substance: 1 mole always contains 6.022 · 10²³ particles – whether atoms, molecules or ions.
q.m10q1.hint: The number starts with 6.022 – and has 23 zeros. How do you write that as a power of ten?
q.m10q2.question: What is the molar mass of water (H₂O)? (H ≈ 1, O ≈ 16 g/mol)
q.m10q2.explanation: M = 2 × 1 + 16 = 18 g/mol. So one mole of water weighs 18 grams.
q.m10q2.hint: M = 2 × M(H) + M(O) = 2 × 1 + 16 – work it out.
q.m10q3.question: 1 mole of any substance weighs the same.
q.m10q3.explanation: False! 1 mole always contains the same number of particles – but the particles have different masses. 1 mol of H₂ ≈ 2 g, 1 mol of O₂ ≈ 32 g.
q.m10q3.hint: The same number of particles – but do hydrogen and oxygen particles weigh the same?
q.m10q4.question: There is 36 g of water (M = 18 g/mol) on the scales. How many moles is that?
q.m10q4.explanation: n = m / M = 36 g / 18 g/mol = 2 mol. Just rearrange the formula m = n · M!
q.m10q4.hint: n = m / M – put in 36 g and 18 g/mol.
q.m10q5.question: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. How many moles of water are formed from 1 mol of O₂?
q.m10q5.explanation: The coefficients read as a mole ratio: 1 mol of O₂ reacts to give 2 mol of H₂O – the “recipe” says so.
q.m10q5.hint: Read the coefficients as a recipe: what is the ratio of 1 mol of O₂ to H₂O?
g.0.def: The state a substance is in: solid, liquid or gaseous. Depends on how much its particles move – that is, on the temperature.
g.1.def: Energy hurdle that particles have to overcome when they collide for a reaction to start. Like a mountain you have to cross – the catalyst builds a tunnel through it.
g.2.def: Elements of group 1 (e.g. sodium, potassium): soft, light and react violently with water. Never found pure in nature because they are so reactive.
g.3.def: Smallest building block of matter that still carries the properties of an element. Structure: heavy nucleus (protons + neutrons) and an almost empty cloud of electrons.
g.4.def: Bond in which two atoms share an electron pair – that way both reach a full outer shell. Typical between non-metals (e.g. H₂, H₂O, CO₂).
g.5.def: Tiny, heavy centre of the atom made of protons and neutrons; contains almost all of the mass.
g.6.def: The number 6.022 · 10²³ (a 6 followed by 23 zeros). It tells you how many particles there are in one mole – whatever the substance.
g.7.def: Opponent of an acid: neutralises it. In water it contains hydroxide ions (OH⁻), pH above 7, often feels soapy-slippery (e.g. soap solution, baking soda).
g.8.def: Separation method: dyes travel across paper at different speeds and so split up into their individual colours. Black ink becomes blue, red and yellow.
g.9.def: Separation method for liquids with different boiling points: you heat the mixture, one substance evaporates first and is collected again as a liquid in a second, cooled vessel.
g.10.def: Starting substance of a reaction – what you put in. Written on the left of the arrow in the reaction equation.
g.11.def: Elements of group 18 (e.g. helium, neon): their outer shell is full – so they form practically no bonds. Ideal for balloons and neon signs.
g.12.def: Tiny, negatively charged particle that whizzes around the atomic nucleus on shells. Almost massless – the mass sits in the nucleus.
g.13.def: The region around the atomic nucleus in which the electrons move on shells. Almost completely empty – the nucleus is tiny in comparison.
g.14.def: Reaction that takes in heat from its surroundings – it gets cold (e.g. a cold pack).
g.15.def: Reaction that gives off heat to its surroundings – it gets warm (e.g. combustion).
g.16.def: Separation method using filter paper: insoluble solids (e.g. sand) get stuck, the liquid runs through.
g.17.def: Several substances that are mixed together but not chemically bonded. Homogeneous (uniform, e.g. salt water) or heterogeneous (components visible, e.g. sand in water).
g.18.def: Vertical column in the periodic table. Elements in a group have the same number of valence electrons – that is why they resemble each other so strongly.
g.19.def: Elements of group 17 (e.g. fluorine, chlorine): reactive non-metals that are exactly 1 electron short of a full shell.
g.20.def: Substance that changes colour depending on the pH value and so shows whether a solution is acidic or basic – e.g. universal indicator or red cabbage juice.
g.21.def: Electrically charged atom or charged group of atoms: if it has given away electrons it is positive (cation, e.g. Na⁺); if it has taken some up it is negative (anion, e.g. Cl⁻ or OH⁻).
g.22.def: Bond through the attraction of opposite charges: a metal gives electrons away (+), a non-metal takes them up (−) – together they hold firmly (e.g. NaCl).
g.23.def: Substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up itself. It lowers the activation energy – like a tunnel through a mountain.
g.24.def: Large number in front of a formula in a reaction equation (e.g. the 2 in 2 H₂O). It counts whole molecules and is adjusted when balancing – never change the small subscripts.
g.25.def: Sum of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of a particular atom – always a whole number. Not to be confused with the atomic mass in the periodic table: that is an average over all isotopes (chlorine: 35.5).
g.26.def: Counting unit for particles: 1 mole = 6.022 · 10²³ particles. That way you do not count atoms one by one but weigh them in huge bundles.
g.27.def: Mass of 1 mole of a substance in grams (g/mol). Simply add up the atomic masses in the formula: H₂O = 2×1 + 16 = 18 g/mol.
g.28.def: Particle made of at least two atoms (e.g. O₂, H₂O, CO₂).
g.29.def: Particle in the atomic nucleus with no charge (neutral). It keeps the nucleus stable and counts towards the mass number.
g.30.def: Acid + base → salt + water. The two opponents cancel each other out and the pH value moves towards 7 (neutral).
g.31.def: Atoms strive for 8 electrons on the outermost shell (noble gas configuration) – the driving force behind all bonds.
g.32.def: Number of protons in the nucleus – it determines which element the atom is and where it sits in the periodic table.
g.33.def: Horizontal row in the periodic table. Its number equals the number of occupied electron shells.
g.34.def: Table of all the elements, ordered by atomic number. If you can read an element's position, you know its properties – like a map of chemistry.
g.35.def: Number from 0 to 14 that measures how acidic or basic something is: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic. Logarithmic: 1 unit of difference = factor of 10.
g.36.def: Substance that is newly formed in a reaction – what comes out. Written on the right of the arrow in the reaction equation.
g.37.def: Positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus. Its number (the atomic number) determines which element the atom is.
g.38.def: Substance that consists of only one kind of particle – e.g. pure water or pure gold. Opposite: mixture.
g.39.def: Substance that releases hydrogen ions (H⁺) in water: pH below 7, tastes sour and can attack materials (e.g. vinegar, lemon juice). Opponent: the base.
g.40.def: States how many moles (bundles of particles) there are – symbol n. Example: 2 mol of water = 2 × 6.022 · 10²³ molecules.
g.41.def: Direct transition from solid to gas without a liquid phase (e.g. dry ice). The reverse path (gas → solid) is called deposition – that is how hoarfrost forms.
g.42.def: Electron on the outermost shell. These few electrons decide how an atom reacts and which bonds it forms.
g.43.def: Substance made of at least two different elements that are firmly bonded chemically (e.g. H₂O, CO₂, NaCl).
g.44.def: Transition liquid → gas; as a separation method it is used to recover dissolved solids (e.g. salt from salt water).
g.45.def: Transition solid → liquid by heating: the particles break free from their fixed positions.
g.46.def: Transition liquid → solid on cooling: the particles settle back into fixed positions.
g.47.def: Transition gas → liquid: the gas particles slow down and settle together. That is how droplets form on a cold window pane.
g.48.def: In every reaction the total mass stays the same: atoms do not disappear and are not newly created – they only swap partners.
g.49.def: Energy level around the nucleus on which electrons move. Shells fill from the inside out: 2 – 8 – 8.
g.50.def: Elements such as carbon, oxygen, chlorine: poor conductors of electricity, often gaseous or brittle. In bonds they take up electrons or share them.
g.51.def: Element with properties between metal and non-metal (e.g. silicon) – important for computer chips.
g.52.def: Another name for the covalent bond: atoms share electron pairs.
g.53.def: Sodium chloride (NaCl), the best-known salt: built from Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that attract each other.
g.54.def: Compound made of positive and negative ions. Formed, for example, from an acid and a base in a neutralisation – table salt is just one example.
g.55.def: Shorthand for the composition of a substance: element symbols plus subscript numbers (e.g. H₂O = 2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen).
g.56.def: Small lowered number in a formula (e.g. the 2 in H₂O). It applies to the element directly before it – no number means 1 atom.
g.57.def: When writing a reaction equation, adjusting the coefficients so that there is the same number of atoms of each element on the left and on the right – never change the subscripts.
g.58.def: Another word for basic: solutions with a pH above 7.
g.59.def: Uniform-looking mixture whose components you cannot see (e.g. salt water, air).
g.60.def: Mixture in which you can make out the components (e.g. sand in water, oil in vinegar).
g.61.def: Temperature at which a substance boils and becomes a gas; the separation principle behind distillation.
g.62.def: Biological catalyst made of protein: speeds up reactions in the body, e.g. in digestion – without being used up itself.
g.63.def: Contact area where particles can meet. The larger it is, the faster the reaction – that is why powder reacts much faster than a lump.
g.64.def: Endothermic process in plants: glucose is made from CO₂ and water using light energy.
g.65.def: Basic idea of chemistry: all substances consist of tiny, constantly moving particles. It explains states of matter and reactions.
g.66.def: Pure basic substance that cannot be broken down any further chemically. All atoms of an element have the same number of protons – that is what makes them belong together.
g.67.def: Elements such as iron, sodium, aluminium: shiny, conduct electricity and heat. In bonds they give electrons away and become positive ions.
g.68.def: Exothermic reaction with oxygen that produces flames. Reactants: fuel + O₂. Products: e.g. CO₂ + H₂O.
g.69.def: Shorthand for a reaction: reactants on the left, products on the right, an arrow in between. Balanced using coefficients.
g.70.def: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons – e.g. carbon-12 (6 neutrons) and carbon-14 (8 neutrons). Chemically they behave the same, only their mass differs.
g.71.def: Mass of an atom in the unit u (1 u ≈ mass of a proton). Shown in the periodic table as the average of all isotopes (chlorine: 35.5 u) and at the same time tells you the molar mass in g/mol.
g.72.def: Abbreviation of an element with one or two letters, the same worldwide: H, O, Na. Some come from Latin – Fe for iron (ferrum), Au for gold (aurum).
g.73.def: Positively charged ion – formed when an atom gives away electrons (e.g. Na⁺, Mg²⁺). Typical for metals.
g.74.def: Negatively charged ion – formed when an atom takes up electrons (e.g. Cl⁻, O²⁻). Typical for non-metals.
g.75.def: Bond between metal atoms: the valence electrons form a freely moving “electron gas” that holds the positive atomic cores together. That is why metals conduct electricity and can be shaped.
g.76.def: Homogeneous mixture of a dissolved substance and a solvent – e.g. salt (dissolved) in water (solvent). Looks uniform but can be separated by evaporation.
g.77.def: States how much of a substance is contained in a given volume – e.g. how many acid particles per litre of solution. The higher the concentration, the more often particles collide.
g.78.def: How fast reactants are converted into products. It increases with temperature, concentration and surface area – and with a catalyst.
labinfo.materie.description: A look into the invisibly small: this lab shows how the particles in solid, liquid and gaseous substances are arranged and how they move. You can see directly why a stone keeps its shape, water flows and air fills every space.
labinfo.materie.howItWorks: Choose a container and move the temperature slider: the particles react immediately – warmer means faster and further apart. In exercise mode you match three particle pictures to the states of matter solid, liquid and gaseous.
labinfo.atome.description: A construction kit for atoms: you decide how many protons, neutrons and electrons your atom has – and see straight away which element it becomes, whether it is neutral or charged (an ion) and how heavy it is.
labinfo.atome.howItWorks: Use the plus and minus buttons to set the number of protons, neutrons and electrons. The display updates live: element, mass number and charge. In exercise mode you build three atoms exactly to specification.
labinfo.periodensystem.description: A hands-on periodic table: click through the elements and discover how groups (vertical) and periods (horizontal) are connected – and what they reveal about the properties of an element.
labinfo.periodensystem.howItWorks: Click an element box to see its profile. Matching colours belong to the same group with similar properties. In exercise mode you find three elements from clues – like a treasure hunt.
labinfo.bindungen.description: Why do atoms stick together? In this lab you combine two substances and watch what happens to their electrons: are they given away and taken up (ionic bond) or shared (covalent bond)?
labinfo.bindungen.howItWorks: Choose a pair of substances – the animation shows the electron transfer or the shared electron pairs step by step. In exercise mode you decide for four pairs of substances which type of bond forms.
labinfo.formeln.description: Read chemical formulas like a pro: this lab breaks real formulas down into their parts and counts with you how many atoms of each element they contain – including the tricky brackets.
labinfo.formeln.howItWorks: The formula is broken down in colour: each colour stands for one element, subscripts and brackets are unpacked visually. In exercise mode you count for yourself in three formulas and enter the numbers of atoms.
labinfo.reaktionen.description: Balancing reaction equations without frustration: you change the coefficients (the large numbers in front of the formulas) and a set of scales shows you immediately whether both sides have the same number of atoms of each kind.
labinfo.reaktionen.howItWorks: Set the coefficients with plus and minus – reactants on the left, products on the right. The scales and the atom count react live. In exercise mode you balance three equations from easy to tricky.
labinfo.ph.description: Acidic, neutral or basic? The virtual pH lab tests twelve everyday substances – from stomach acid to sodium hydroxide solution – and colours the display to match the pH scale.
labinfo.ph.howItWorks: Choose a substance and read off its pH value, colour and classification: below 7 is acidic, around 7 neutral, above 7 basic. Every pH step means a factor of 10! In exercise mode you sort five substances into the right ranges.
labinfo.trennung.description: Getting mixtures of substances apart again – chemists can do that with four classic methods: filtering, evaporating, distilling and the magnet. This lab shows which method works when, and why.
labinfo.trennung.howItWorks: Choose a mixture and a method and watch the animation: does something stay in the filter? Does the water evaporate? The trick is always a property of the substance, such as grain size or boiling point. In exercise mode you separate four mixtures correctly.
labinfo.energie.description: Make the reaction as fast as you like: magnesium reacts with acid – and you control how fiercely it fizzes via temperature, concentration and degree of division. An energy diagram shows you what is going on behind the scenes.
labinfo.energie.howItWorks: Set the three controls and start the reaction – a timer measures how long it takes, and the energy diagram shows the activation energy as a "mountain". In exercise mode you tinker until the reaction is finished in just 1 second.
labinfo.mol.description: The mole scale translates between the world of particles and everyday lab work: you see how grams are converted into moles – and why 1 mole of water weighs 18 g but 1 mole of gold almost 200 g.
labinfo.mol.howItWorks: Choose a substance and enter a mass or an amount of substance – the scale converts instantly using m = n · M. In exercise mode you solve four calculations from the lab ticket, from converting units to reading an equation as a recipe.

lab.periodic.clue.hunt1: I am the noble gas in period 2 – neon signs need me for their red glow.

lab.bond.ionicTitle: Ionic bond: how table salt is formed
lab.bond.atomicTitle: Covalent bond: sharing instead of swapping (H₂)
lab.bond.naclDone: NaCl – the ions hold firmly together
lab.bond.nastep1.title: Starting point
lab.bond.nastep1.text: Sodium (Na) has 1 lone valence electron – it wants to get rid of it. Chlorine (Cl) has 7 – it is exactly 1 short of a full shell.
lab.bond.nastep2.title: Electron transfer
lab.bond.nastep2.text: Sodium hands its valence electron over to chlorine. That way both reach a full outer shell (octet rule).
lab.bond.nastep3.title: Ions are formed
lab.bond.nastep3.text: Sodium now has 1 electron fewer than protons → Na⁺. Chlorine has 1 electron more → Cl⁻. Neutral atoms have become charged ions.
lab.bond.nastep4.title: Ionic bond
lab.bond.nastep4.text: Opposite charges attract: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ cling firmly to each other. And there you have table salt, NaCl!
lab.bond.h2step1: Two single hydrogen atoms: each has only 1 electron – the first shell would be full with 2.
lab.bond.h2step2: The atoms approach each other. Neither wants to give up its electron – after all, both need one more!
lab.bond.h2step3: The answer: they share! Each contributes 1 electron to a shared electron pair. That way each atom gets 2 electrons. And there you have H₂!
lab.bond.why.bondwhy1: Sodium (metal) hands an electron over to chlorine (non-metal) → Na⁺ and Cl⁻ attract each other.
lab.bond.why.bondwhy2: Both are non-metals and share an electron pair → H₂.
lab.bond.why.bondwhy3: Magnesium hands 2 electrons over to oxygen → Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ (magnesium oxide).
lab.bond.why.bondwhy4: Carbon and oxygen share electron pairs → e.g. CO₂.
lab.bond.wrong: Not quite. Ask yourself: does a metal give its electron away, or do two non-metals share?
lab.bond.done: All bond types correct – you are a true bond builder! 🎉

lab.formula.wrongPlain: Not yet. Count subscript by subscript.
lab.formula.wrongBracket: Not yet. Count subscript by subscript – and remember: everything inside the bracket occurs 2 times!
lab.formula.desc.fx1: 2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen – the most famous molecule in the world.
lab.formula.desc.fx2: 1 carbon + 2 oxygen – formed when we breathe and when things burn.
lab.formula.desc.fx3: 1 nitrogen + 3 hydrogen – found in cleaning products and fertiliser.
lab.formula.desc.fx4: 6 carbon + 12 hydrogen + 6 oxygen – energy for your cells.
lab.formula.desc.fx5: The bracket counts twice: 1 calcium + 2 oxygen + 2 hydrogen.
lab.eq.title: How to read a reaction equation
lab.eq.educts: are on the left: the starting substances (hydrogen, oxygen).
lab.eq.arrow: means “reacts to form” – the direction of the reaction.
lab.eq.products: are on the right: what is newly formed (water).
lab.eq.coefNote: The large number in front (the coefficient) counts whole molecules: 2 H₂O = 2 water molecules. The small subscript number belongs to the atom – it must never be changed when balancing!
lab.eq.instruction: Set the coefficients so that there is the same number of atoms of each element on the left and on the right.
lab.eq.wrong: The balance is not right yet – look at the atom counters above and work out which coefficient is missing.
lab.eq.reducible: The balance is already correct! But chemists use the smallest possible whole numbers: divide all coefficients by {g}.
lab.ph.colorNote: The colour shows the universal indicator: red = acidic, green = neutral, violet = basic.

lab.sep.note.mixnote2: The water evaporates – the salt is left behind as white crystals.
lab.sep.note.mixnote3: The magnet pulls out the iron filings, the sand stays behind.

lab.sep.wrong: Think: which property sets the substances apart – size, boiling point or magnetism?
lab.sep.done: All mixtures separated correctly – master class! 🎉
lab.energy.exoDesc: The products lie lower than the reactants: the difference is released as heat – it gets hot (burning, hand warmers).
lab.energy.endoDesc: The products lie higher than the reactants: the reaction draws energy from its surroundings – it gets cold (cold pack).
lab.energy.tunerIntro: Set the conditions and watch the gas bubbles: the more bubbles per second, the faster the reaction.
lab.energy.tooSlow: Still too slow. Not at maximum: {missing}. Think with the particle model: what gives more collisions per second?
lab.energy.done: 1 second – full speed! You have understood all three levers. 🎉
